pois.name: Richmond Castle

metadata.description: Norman castle built in 1071, one of the oldest stone castles in England

visual_cues: Massive stone keep rising 100 feet above the town
Thick castle walls made of local limestone
Arched Norman gateway entrance
Towers visible from the market square
facts: Richmond Castle was built starting in 1071 by Alan Rufus, a Breton nobleman who fought at the Battle of Hastings. It's one of the oldest Norman stone fortresses in Britain.
The castle's 100-foot-tall keep, called Scotland's Hall, is one of the finest examples of 11th-century architecture in England and offers panoramic views of the Yorkshire Dales.

During World War I, the castle was used as a prison for conscientious objectors. 16 men who refused military service were held here before being sent to France and sentenced to death (later commuted).

pois.name: Greyfriars Tower

metadata.description: 15th-century bell tower, sole remnant of Franciscan friary

visual_cues: Solitary square stone tower standing alone
Gothic-style arched windows
Weathered grey stone
Small arched doorway at ground level
facts: Greyfriars Tower is all that remains of a Franciscan friary founded in 1258. The friars lived here for nearly 300 years until Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries in 1539.
The tower you see today was built around 1500 as the friary's bell tower. After the Dissolution, it was converted into a private dwelling and later used as a courthouse.
Local legend claims the tower is haunted by the ghost of a grey friar who walks the grounds at night, still ringing the bells that no longer exist.

pois.name: Richmond Market Place

metadata.description: Historic cobbled market square, one of the largest in England

visual_cues: Large cobblestone square
Tall stone obelisk in the center
Colorful Georgian buildings surrounding the square
Market stalls on weekends
Castle visible on the hill to the east
facts: Richmond's Market Place has been the commercial heart of the town since 1071, when the castle was built. Markets have been held here continuously for over 950 years.
The cobbled square is one of the largest market places in England, covering nearly 4 acres. It was deliberately built large to accommodate the massive livestock markets that made Richmond wealthy.
The Market Cross obelisk in the center dates from 1771. It replaced an earlier medieval cross where public proclamations were read and punishments carried out.

pois.name: The Georgian Theatre Royal

metadata.description: Built in 1788, Britain's most complete Georgian playhouse

visual_cues: Narrow Georgian townhouse facade
Small arched entrance doorway
Cream-colored stone building
Period window frames
Tucked into Victoria Road near the market
facts: Built in 1788 by actor-manager Samuel Butler, this is Britain's most complete Georgian playhouse. It closed in 1848 and was forgotten until its rediscovery in 1960.
When restoration began in 1963, they found the original painted scenery, 200-year-old playbills, and even the actor's dressing rooms intact—like a theatrical time capsule.
The theatre has a capacity of just 214 people and still uses candle-lit performances to recreate the authentic Georgian atmosphere. The stage is only 15 feet wide.

pois.name: Richmondshire Museum

metadata.description: Local history museum in former church building

visual_cues: Red brick building on Ryder's Wynd
Small entrance with museum sign
Traditional shop-front windows
Near the marketplace
facts: The museum is housed in an old joiner's shop and tells the story of Richmond and the surrounding dales. It includes a recreated Victorian street and a collection of agricultural tools.
One of the museum's most unusual exhibits is James Herriot's original veterinary surgery set from the TV series 'All Creatures Great and Small,' which was filmed in the area.
The museum also houses military artifacts from the Yorkshire Regiment and exhibits on the town's lead mining heritage, which brought wealth to Richmond in the 18th and 19th centuries.

pois.name: St Mary's Church

metadata.description: Medieval parish church with Victorian restoration

visual_cues: Square stone bell tower
Gothic arched entrance
Large stained glass windows
Stone walls with ivy
Graveyard with old headstones
facts: St Mary's Parish Church dates back to at least 1135, making it one of Richmond's oldest buildings. The tower and much of the structure are from the 12th century.
During the 1850s, the church underwent major Victorian restoration. However, parts of the original Norman church remain, including several medieval grave slabs set into the floor.
The church graveyard contains graves of soldiers from the nearby Catterick Garrison, including Commonwealth War Graves from both World Wars.

pois.name: The Green Howards Regimental Museum

metadata.description: Military museum covering 300 years of Yorkshire regiment history

visual_cues: Former church building with tower
Military flags and banners outside
Stone Gothic architecture
Green Howards Museum sign
Trinity Church Square location
facts: The Green Howards Regiment was formed in 1688 and served in virtually every major British conflict for 316 years, including Waterloo, the Somme, and D-Day, before being merged in 2006.
The museum displays over 300 years of military history including 18 Victoria Crosses—Britain's highest award for valor. One was won by a 14-year-old drummer boy.
The regiment's nickname 'Green Howards' came from their green facings and their colonel, Charles Howard, to distinguish them from another regiment also led by a Howard.

pois.name: Richmond Bridge

metadata.description: Medieval stone bridge over River Swale, dating from 1789

visual_cues: Single stone arch bridge
Pale stone construction
River Swale flowing beneath
View of the castle from the bridge
Steep banks on either side
facts: Richmond Bridge was built in 1789 to replace an older medieval bridge. It has a single elegant arch spanning 112 feet across the River Swale.
The bridge was designed by a local mason and was built for £2,500—quite expensive for its time. A toll was charged to cross until 1846 to recoup the construction costs.
The Swale below is one of England's fastest-flowing rivers. In flood conditions, the water can rise 15 feet and surge under the bridge with tremendous force.

pois.name: Richmond Falls

metadata.description: Series of waterfalls on the River Swale beneath the castle

visual_cues: Cascading water over rock ledges
River flowing fast with white water
Wooded banks
Castle walls rising above on the cliff
Stone steps leading down to the water
facts: Richmond Falls is a series of small waterfalls and rapids on the River Swale, just below the castle. The Swale is one of the fastest rivers in England.
The falls are particularly dramatic after heavy rain, when the water level can rise several feet in hours. Victorian tourists would come specifically to see the falls in flood.
The riverbank path offers views of the castle perched on the cliff above—this is the classic Richmond postcard view that's been photographed for over 150 years.

pois.name: The Old Brewery

metadata.description: 19th-century brewery building, now converted to residential and commercial use

visual_cues: Tall stone industrial building with multiple floors
Large arched windows typical of Victorian breweries
Converted warehouse aesthetic with modern additions
Located near the marketplace on a sloping street
Distinctive chimney or ventilation tower
facts: Richmond had several breweries in the 18th and 19th centuries, serving the town's many coaching inns and the nearby Catterick military garrison. At its peak, the town had at least three active breweries.
The brewing industry in Richmond declined in the early 20th century as national breweries consolidated and railways made it cheaper to transport beer from larger operations elsewhere.
Many of Richmond's former brewery buildings have been converted to other uses, preserving their distinctive industrial architecture with high ceilings and large windows designed for ventilation.

pois.name: Millgate House Gardens

metadata.description: Award-winning terraced garden near castle with stunning views

visual_cues: Georgian townhouse with walled garden entrance
Terraced gardens stepping down the hillside
Views of the castle and River Swale below
Abundant roses and climbing plants on stone walls
Narrow gate on Millgate street
facts: Millgate House Gardens has won multiple awards including the prestigious Good Gardens Guide 'Garden of the Year'. The garden tumbles down a steep hillside with views of Richmond Castle and the River Swale.

The garden was created over decades by owners Austin Lynch and Tim Culkin, who transformed a neglected slope into one of England's most celebrated small gardens, featured in numerous gardening publications.
The terraced design uses the challenging steep site to create intimate garden 'rooms', each with a different character—from formal rose gardens to wild woodland plantings clinging to the cliff edge.

pois.name: Trinity Church Square

metadata.description: Former Holy Trinity Church, now community venue and cultural space

visual_cues: Georgian church building with classical portico
Tall arched windows along the sides
Small square with benches in front
Stone steps leading to columned entrance
Clock tower or bell cupola on roof
facts: Holy Trinity Church was built in 1837 during the Georgian era to serve Richmond's growing population. The elegant classical design reflects the architectural tastes of the period.
The church was declared redundant in 1971 and later converted into a community space. It now hosts concerts, exhibitions, and cultural events, giving the historic building new life.
Trinity Church Square, the small plaza in front, provides one of Richmond's quieter public spaces—a pleasant contrast to the busier Market Place just a short walk away.

pois.name: Culloden Tower

metadata.description: 18th-century Gothic folly built to commemorate Battle of Culloden

visual_cues: Tall octagonal stone tower standing alone on a hillside
Gothic-style pointed arch windows
Crenellated top like a miniature castle
Honey-colored stone exterior
Visible from town across the valley
facts: Culloden Tower was built in 1746 by John Yorke to commemorate the Duke of Cumberland's victory at the Battle of Culloden, which ended the Jacobite Rising and Bonnie Prince Charlie's claim to the throne.
The tower stands about 60 feet tall and was designed as a banqueting house where Yorke could entertain guests while enjoying panoramic views over his estate and the River Swale valley.
It's an early example of Gothic Revival architecture, built decades before the style became fashionable. The Landmark Trust restored the building, and it can now be rented as a holiday cottage.

pois.name: The Bar

metadata.description: Medieval archway and former toll gate marking the old town boundary

visual_cues: Stone archway spanning the narrow street
Building constructed above the arch
Narrow passage for pedestrians and vehicles
Worn stone at the base from centuries of use
Street slopes steeply on either side
facts: The Bar is one of Richmond's oldest surviving structures, dating back to the medieval period. It marked the boundary of the town and controlled access to the marketplace.
Originally a toll gate, merchants and traders would have paid fees here to bring goods into Richmond's market. The building above the arch was likely used by the toll collector.
The narrow archway gives a sense of the compact, fortified nature of medieval Richmond, where thick walls and controlled entry points provided security for the town's valuable market trade.

pois.name: Richmond Station

metadata.description: Beautifully restored Victorian railway station, now cinema, cafe, and heritage center

visual_cues: Long Victorian stone building with decorative canopy
Original platform with heritage railway carriages
Ornate ironwork and period lamp posts
Arched windows and station clock
Café tables on the former platform
facts: Richmond Station opened in 1846 as the terminus of the branch line from Darlington. It served the town for over 120 years before closing in 1969 during the Beeching cuts that decimated Britain's rural railways.
The station sat derelict for decades before a major restoration project transformed it into a cultural hub. It now houses a two-screen cinema, artisan food hall, bakery, and ice cream shop.

The restoration preserved many original features including the platform, canopy, and Victorian architectural details. Heritage railway carriages on the platform add to the authentic atmosphere and house additional shops.
